subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: What is a globe?
options: A true model of the Earth, showing its shape and the position of places on it
A flat map of the world printed on paper
A model of the solar system
hint: Unlike a flat map, a globe does not distort the shapes of continents.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions

options: The path the Earth follows around the Sun
An imaginary line passing through the centre of the Earth from the North Pole to the South Pole
A real rod running through the planet
hint: It is imaginary — you would not find it if you dug down.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: The Earth's axis is tilted. By how much?
options: It is not tilted at all
hint: The same tilt is often given as 66½° from the plane of the orbit.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Why does a globe sit at a slant on its stand?
options: Because it makes the globe easier to spin
Because it shows the Earth's real tilt, which is fixed as it travels round the Sun
Because the Earth wobbles from side to side
Because the maker fixed it badly
hint: The slant is the whole reason the seasons exist.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Which imaginary line divides the Earth into two equal halves?
hint: It runs exactly midway between the two poles.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: What is the shape of the Earth?
options: Slightly flattened at the poles and bulging at the equator
hint: The word geographers use is 'geoid' — earth-shaped.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: What is the main advantage of a globe over a flat map?
options: It shows the size, shape and distance of places without distortion
It shows more detail of small areas
It can be folded and carried easily
hint: You cannot flatten a curved surface without stretching something.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: What is the main disadvantage of a globe?
options: It cannot show a small area in detail and is not easy to carry about
It shows the wrong shapes for continents
It shows only one hemisphere at a time
hint: You would not use one to find a street.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: The needle on which a globe turns represents what?
hint: The globe spins about it just as the Earth spins about its axis.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Which two points on the Earth do not move when the Earth rotates?
options: The points where the Prime Meridian meets the equator
The North Pole and the South Pole
hint: The axis passes through them, so they turn on the spot.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Why is the equator called the zero-degree parallel?
options: Because it is the shortest parallel
It is the starting line from which latitude is measured to the north and to the south
Because no country lies on it
Because the temperature there is zero
hint: Every other parallel is measured as an angle from it.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: If the Earth's axis were not tilted, what would happen?
options: The Earth would move closer to the Sun
There would be no day and night
Day and night would be nearly equal all year and there would be no seasons as we know them
hint: Tilt is what makes one hemisphere lean towards the Sun at a time.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: What does the plane of the Earth's orbit mean?
options: The line joining the two poles
The surface of the Earth itself
The path of an aeroplane over the Earth
The flat surface in which the Earth travels around the Sun
hint: The axis is tilted 66½° to this plane.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Which of these is true of the equator?
options: It is the shortest parallel of latitude
It is the longest parallel of latitude
hint: The circles get smaller as you move towards the poles.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Which continent does the equator NOT pass through?
hint: It passes through Indonesia in Asia, but Australia lies wholly south of it.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: A globe shows the world in what proportion to the real Earth?
options: Larger than life for the oceans only
To scale, so that relative sizes and distances are correct
With no fixed relationship at all
hint: A globe is a scale model, like a model aeroplane.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Why can no flat map of the whole world be completely accurate?
options: Because the Earth is always moving
A curved surface cannot be flattened without stretching or tearing some part of it
hint: Try flattening an orange peel and see what happens to it.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: What are the two poles of the Earth called?
options: The North Pole and the South Pole
The magnetic pole and the geographic pole
The east pole and the west pole
The upper pole and the lower pole
hint: They are the two points where the axis meets the surface.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: What lies at 90° North?
hint: 90° is the greatest latitude possible.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Why do we need imaginary lines on the globe at all?
options: Because they mark real boundaries between countries
Because without a system of reference there is no way to state exactly where a place is
Because they show where the Earth is thickest
Because they can be seen from space
hint: The lines are a language for describing position.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: What is a parallel of latitude?
options: A line marking a country's border
The path of the Sun across the sky
A circle drawn around the globe parallel to the equator
A line joining the North Pole to the South Pole
hint: They never meet, which is why they are called parallels.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: What is the latitude of the equator?
hint: It is the line from which all other latitudes are measured.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: The equator divides the Earth into which two hemispheres?
hint: North and south are measured from the equator.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: What is the latitude of the Tropic of Cancer?
hint: Cancer lies north of the equator; Capricorn lies south.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: What is the latitude of the Tropic of Capricorn?
hint: It is the mirror image of the Tropic of Cancer.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: What is the latitude of the Arctic Circle?
hint: The Antarctic Circle is its counterpart in the south.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: As you move away from the equator towards a pole, what happens to the parallels?
options: They stay exactly the same length
They begin to cross one another
hint: Picture the circles shrinking towards the top of an orange.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Why can latitude never be more than 90°?
options: Because beyond 90° the parallels become meridians
Because the Earth has only 90 parallels
Because 90 is the largest number used in geography
Because 90° is the angle from the equator to the pole, and the pole is as far as you can go
hint: The angle is measured from the centre of the Earth.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Delhi is at about 28° North. What does this tell you?
options: It is 28 degrees above sea level
It is 28 kilometres from the equator
It lies about 28 degrees north of the equator
It lies 28 degrees east of Greenwich
hint: Latitude is an angle, not a distance in kilometres.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Which hemisphere is India in?
options: Partly in both, with the equator running through it
Neither, since it lies on the equator
hint: The whole of mainland India lies north of the equator.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: If parallels of latitude are drawn at intervals of one degree, how many are there in all?
hint: Ninety in the north, ninety in the south, and the equator itself.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Roughly how far apart are two parallels one degree apart?
hint: It is nearly the same everywhere, because the parallels are evenly spaced.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Which of these places is closest to the equator?
hint: The smaller the number, the closer to the equator, north or south.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Why are latitudes important for understanding climate?
options: They tell you how directly the Sun's rays strike a place, which affects how hot it is
They indicate the height of the land
They mark the boundaries of countries
They show how much rain a place receives
hint: Near the equator the rays fall almost straight down; near the poles they slant.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Two places lie at the same latitude but on opposite sides of the Earth. What do they share?
options: The same distance from the equator, and broadly similar sunlight through the year
hint: Latitude fixes the Sun's angle; longitude fixes the time.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Which important parallel passes through India?
hint: It runs across the middle of the country, through eight states.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: What is the latitude of the South Pole?
hint: It is the furthest south any place can be.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Which statement about parallels is correct?
options: They are all of equal length
They are semicircles that meet at the poles
They are complete circles and never meet one another
They run from north to south
hint: Compare them with meridians, which do meet at the poles.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: A ship sails due east along a parallel. What stays the same?
hint: Sailing along a parallel means keeping the same distance from the equator.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Why is the equator the longest parallel?
options: It is closest to the Sun
It is drawn around the widest part of the Earth
It passes through the most countries
It is the only parallel that is a full circle
hint: The Earth bulges at the equator.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: What is a meridian of longitude?
options: A semicircle running from the North Pole to the South Pole
A circle drawn parallel to the equator
A line marking the edge of a time zone only
The path of the Moon across the sky
hint: All meridians meet at both poles.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Through which place does the Prime Meridian pass?
hint: The old Royal Observatory there gave the line its name.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: What is the longitude of the Prime Meridian?
hint: It is the starting line for measuring longitude east and west.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: What is the greatest possible longitude?
hint: Going 180° either way from Greenwich brings you to the same meridian.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: How do meridians differ from parallels?
options: Meridians are circles and parallels are semicircles
Meridians are all of equal length and meet at the poles; parallels differ in length and never meet
hint: Two differences: length, and whether they meet.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: If meridians are drawn at intervals of one degree, how many are there in all?
hint: 180 to the east and 180 to the west, counting 0° and 180° once each.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Delhi is at about 77° East. What does this mean?
options: It lies in the Western Hemisphere
It lies about 77 degrees east of the Prime Meridian
It is 77 degrees north of the equator
hint: East and west are always measured from Greenwich.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: The 0° and 180° meridians together divide the Earth into which hemispheres?
hint: Latitude gives north and south; longitude gives east and west.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Why is Greenwich, rather than any other place, the site of the Prime Meridian?
options: Because it lies exactly at the centre of the Earth
It was chosen by international agreement in the nineteenth century, not for any natural reason
Because the Sun rises there first
Because it is the oldest city in the world
hint: Any meridian could have been chosen; the world simply had to agree on one.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: What happens to the distance between two meridians as you travel towards a pole?
options: It becomes smaller, until the meridians meet at the pole
hint: They are furthest apart at the equator.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Which of these is true of all meridians?
options: They run parallel to the equator
hint: Each is half of a great circle passing through both poles.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: India's easternmost and westernmost points differ by about 30° of longitude. What does this cause?
options: A difference of about two degrees in temperature
A difference in the date between the two ends
A difference of about two hours in local time across the country
hint: Fifteen degrees is one hour, so thirty degrees is two.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Which meridian lies exactly opposite the Prime Meridian?
hint: Together they form one complete circle around the Earth.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: A place is at 20° West. In which hemisphere does it lie?
hint: West of Greenwich means the Western Hemisphere.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Why are meridians useful for measuring time?
options: Because the Sun travels along them
Because they are drawn on every clock
Because they mark the borders of countries
Because the Earth turns through a fixed number of degrees each hour
hint: The Earth turns 360° in 24 hours.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Which two things together fix the exact position of any place on Earth?
options: Its latitude and its height above sea level
Its longitude and its distance from the nearest city
Its time zone and its climate
hint: One number gives north-south, the other east-west.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Meridians are sometimes called lines of longitude. What does 'longitude' measure?
options: The angular distance of a place east or west of the Prime Meridian
The distance of a place from the North Pole
The height of a place above the sea
The length of a country from end to end
hint: Like latitude, it is measured as an angle.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Why does no place have a longitude of 200°?
options: Because 200° would be inside the Earth
Because such places are too far away
Because longitude is measured only up to 180° in each direction from Greenwich
hint: Beyond 180° east you have started coming back west.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Two towns lie on the same meridian, one far north of the other. What do they share?
hint: Local time depends on longitude alone.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: What is a great circle?
options: The orbit of the Earth around the Sun
A circle around the Tropic of Cancer
Any circle drawn on a globe
Any circle that divides the Earth into two equal halves
hint: The equator is one; so is any pair of opposite meridians joined together.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: What is the Earth grid?
options: The network formed when parallels of latitude cross meridians of longitude
The system of roads across a country
The framework holding a globe on its stand
hint: It is a net of imaginary lines used to locate places.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: When giving the position of a place, which is stated first?
hint: Latitude first, then longitude — north-south before east-west.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: A place is described as 19° N, 73° E. Where is it?
options: North of the equator and west of Greenwich
South of the equator and west of Greenwich
North of the equator and east of the Prime Meridian
hint: Read the two letters: N for the hemisphere, E for the side of Greenwich.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Why is the grid necessary for a ship at sea?
options: There are no landmarks, so a position can only be given as a pair of coordinates
Because the sea has no water currents
hint: In mid-ocean, coordinates are the only address there is.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Which of these gives a complete location?
hint: You need both numbers and both directions.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: What would happen if a location gave only the latitude?
options: The place would be exactly located anyway
The place could be anywhere along that whole circle around the Earth
The place would be at the North Pole
hint: One number narrows it to a circle, not a point.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: How is a degree divided for a more exact position?
options: Into 60 minutes, and each minute into 60 seconds
hint: It works like an hour on a clock.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: The standard meridian of India is 82° 30' E. What does the 30' mean?
options: Thirty minutes, which is half a degree
hint: Sixty minutes make one degree, so 30' is a half.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Which pair of coordinates would be found in the Southern Hemisphere?
hint: Look only at the first letter.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Why do maps and globes both use the same grid?
options: Because the grid shows political borders
So that a place has the same coordinates whichever one you use
Because it makes them cheaper to print
Because the lines are visible from space
hint: A shared system means a position can be exchanged between them.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Two places have the same longitude but different latitudes. What follows?
options: They share the same local time but not the same climate
They share the same climate but not the same time
hint: Longitude governs time; latitude governs the Sun's angle.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Where on the grid do all the meridians meet?
hint: That is why a pole has a latitude but no useful longitude.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Why does a place at the North Pole have no meaningful longitude?
options: Because every meridian passes through it
Because it is covered in ice
hint: You cannot say which meridian you are on if you are on all of them.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: A search party is told a missing boat is at 12° N, 75° E. Why is this useful?
options: It gives the boat's direction of travel
It tells them the weather at the spot
It tells them how deep the sea is there
It gives one exact point on the Earth's surface to search
hint: The grid turns 'somewhere in the Arabian Sea' into a point.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: What do we call the imaginary lines that run east to west around the globe?
hint: They run east-west but measure north-south position.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Why is it wrong to say the grid lines are real lines on the ground?
options: They are imaginary; they exist only as a system of measurement
They are real but visible only from aircraft
They are real but painted only on the oceans
They are real boundaries between countries
hint: You could stand on the equator and see nothing on the ground.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Which coordinate changes when you travel due north?
hint: Travelling north means moving away from the equator.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Which coordinate changes when you travel due west?
hint: East and west are measured by longitude.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: How does a modern navigation system use the grid?
options: It measures the distance to the nearest town
It does not use the grid at all
It reads the grid lines painted on the road
It calculates the receiver's latitude and longitude and shows it on a map
hint: Satellite navigation gives coordinates first, and the map is drawn from them.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: What is the strongest reason the world agreed on one grid system?
options: So that every country could have its own meridian
Because the United Nations required it
So that a position stated in one country means exactly the same thing in every other
hint: Navigation across the world depends on a shared language of position.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: How many heat zones is the Earth divided into?

Three kinds — the Torrid, the Temperate and the Frigid
Four kinds, one for each season
hint: There is one Torrid Zone, two Temperate and two Frigid.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Between which two lines does the Torrid Zone lie?
options: The equator and the Tropic of Cancer
The Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn
The Arctic Circle and the North Pole
The Arctic Circle and the Antarctic Circle
hint: It is the band on either side of the equator.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Why is the Torrid Zone the hottest?
options: It has the least cloud cover
The Sun is directly overhead there at least once a year, so its rays are most concentrated
It is the part of the Earth closest to the Sun
It receives sunlight for more hours than anywhere else
hint: The angle of the rays matters far more than the distance.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Where does the North Temperate Zone lie?
options: Between the Arctic Circle and the North Pole
Between the Tropic of Cancer and the Arctic Circle
Between the equator and the Tropic of Cancer
hint: Temperate means moderate — neither extreme.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Where does the Frigid Zone of the north lie?
options: Between the Tropic of Cancer and the Arctic Circle
Between the Arctic Circle and the North Pole
Around the whole of the Northern Hemisphere
Between the equator and the Tropic of Cancer
hint: Frigid means very cold.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Why are the Frigid Zones so cold?
options: They are covered in cloud all year
They are furthest from the Sun
The Sun's rays always strike them at a slant, so their heat is spread thinly
They never receive any sunlight at all
hint: A torch shone at a slant lights a larger, dimmer patch.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: In which heat zone does most of India lie?
hint: The Tropic of Cancer runs across the middle of the country.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Which heat zone has the most moderate temperatures?
hint: The name gives it away.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Why does the Sun never shine directly overhead in the Temperate Zones?
options: Because the Earth's axis points away from them
Because the Sun is only ever overhead between the two tropics
Because those zones are always cloudy
Because they are too far from the equator to receive sunlight
hint: The tilt of 23½° sets the limit of the overhead Sun.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: What is the connection between the heat zones and the Earth's tilt?
options: The tilt fixes the tropics and the polar circles, which are the boundaries of the zones
The tilt decides the temperature directly
There is no connection between them
hint: 23½° and 66½° are both consequences of the same tilt.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: In the Frigid Zones, what unusual thing happens for part of the year?
options: There is no sunlight at any time of year
The Sun rises in the west
Day and night are always equal
The Sun does not set for some weeks in summer, or does not rise for some weeks in winter
hint: This is why Norway is called the land of the midnight Sun.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Which zone receives the most direct sunlight through the year?
hint: Direct means striking the ground close to straight down.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: A place lies at 50° North. Which zone is it in?
hint: It lies between 23½° N and 66½° N.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: A place lies at 70° South. Which zone is it in?
hint: It lies beyond the Antarctic Circle at 66½° S.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Why do very few people live in the Frigid Zones?
options: Governments do not allow settlement there
The zones are entirely covered by ocean
The extreme cold makes farming and ordinary life very difficult
There is no land in those zones
hint: Where nothing grows, few people settle.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Which heat zone supports the greatest variety of plant life?
options: All zones support the same variety
The Torrid Zone, with its heat and heavy rainfall
hint: The great rainforests all lie in this band.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: How many Temperate Zones are there, and why?
options: Two — one in each hemisphere, between the tropic and the polar circle
hint: The pattern of zones repeats on either side of the equator.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Which line marks the boundary between the Torrid and the South Temperate Zone?
hint: It lies at 23½° South.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Why is the heat zone of a place a better guide to its temperature than its longitude?
options: Because the zone depends on latitude, which decides how directly the Sun's rays fall
Because longitude changes with the seasons
Because longitude is harder to measure
hint: Longitude tells you the time, not the temperature.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Two places lie at the same latitude but one is much colder. What could explain this?
options: One may be far higher above sea level, or far from the sea
One must be in a different heat zone
One must be closer to the Sun
hint: Heat zones give the broad pattern; height and distance from the sea modify it.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: What is local time?
options: The time kept by a local radio station
The time at a place decided by the position of the Sun in its sky
The time shown on a country's official clocks
The time at the Prime Meridian
hint: It is noon by local time when the Sun is highest.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: What is standard time?
options: The time kept only by railways
The average of every local time in the world
One time chosen for a whole country or region, based on a single meridian
hint: Without it, every town would keep a slightly different clock.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Why do countries adopt a standard time instead of using local time everywhere?
options: Because different clocks in every town would make travel, trade and timetables impossible
Because clocks cannot be set accurately
Because local time cannot be measured
hint: Railways were the first to demand a single time.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: What does GMT stand for?
hint: It is the time at the 0° meridian.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Which meridian is used for Indian Standard Time?
hint: It passes near Mirzapur in Uttar Pradesh.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: How far ahead of GMT is Indian Standard Time?

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Why is Indian Standard Time ahead of GMT rather than behind it?
options: Because India lies east of Greenwich, and the Sun rises there earlier
Because India chose to be ahead
Because India is nearer the equator
Because India is a larger country than Britain
hint: East means earlier; the Earth turns from west to east.

subject: social-science
chapter: The Earth: Globe, Time and Motions
question: Which of these countries needs more than one standard time?
options: Nepal, which lies in the mountains

options: Because summer happens at the same time everywhere
Both hemispheres would then have summer at the same time, and they do not
Because the Sun does not give out heat
Because the Earth's distance from the Sun never changes
hint: December is summer in Australia and winter in India, on the same day.

Because its part of the Earth stays in sunlight for more of each rotation in summer
Because the Sun moves more slowly there

options: Kanyakumari, because it lies near the sea
Srinagar, because it lies much further north
Kanyakumari, because it is nearer the equator
hint: The further from the equator, the greater the swing.

question: Why is the length of the day in Chennai almost the same in June and December?
options: Because Chennai is on the coast
Because Chennai lies in the Frigid Zone
Because Chennai keeps a different standard time
Because Chennai lies close to the equator, where daylight changes very little
hint: Latitude, not longitude, decides the swing.

options: It has no effect on the length of day
It marks the boundary of the Torrid Zone
It shows where the Sun is overhead
It divides the lit half from the dark half, and where it cuts a latitude decides how long that place stays in sunlight
hint: The tilt makes it cut most latitudes unevenly.

question: Why do days grow longer in the Northern Hemisphere between December and June?
options: Because the Earth is speeding up
Because the Northern Hemisphere is tilting further towards the Sun over those months
Because the Earth is coming closer to the Sun
Because the axis is becoming more upright
hint: The tilt is fixed; what changes is where the Earth is in its orbit.

Their days are of nearly the same length, though they begin at different moments
One has day while the other has night for the whole year
Their days differ by exactly twelve hours
hint: Latitude sets the length; longitude sets the timing.

question: How does the varying length of day affect life in far northern countries?
options: It causes the seasons to reverse
It has no effect on daily life
Work, school and sleep must be arranged around very long summer days and very dark winters
It changes the language people speak
hint: In some towns children go to school in the dark for months.

question: What single fact explains both the seasons and the varying length of day and night?

The Earth's orbit is an ellipse
The Earth spins from west to east
The Earth's axis is tilted as it revolves around the Sun
hint: One tilt, two consequences.
